raw_case_text:
The patient is a 66-year-old female with a past medical history significant for hypertension, seizure disorder, and hydrocephalus status-post ventricular-pleural (VP) shunt that came to the emergency department due to altered mental status. The patient had hydrocephalus due to cerebellar tumor with leptomeningeal metastases diagnosed by tissue sample 20 years ago, complicated with compressive hydrocephalus and ventriculomegaly that was only treated with a VP shunt, and there is no information of other treatment options. At baseline, the patient is bed-bound, alert, and oriented to person, time, and lives in a nursing home. She was brought due to fluctuation in her mental status, inattention, nonverbal response, and multiple febrile episodes with a maximum temperature of 101.4 F (38.5 C) of 2 days of duration. History was limited due to the inability of the patient to provide additional information. She was recently admitted to the hospital two months ago due to the concern of gastrointestinal bleeding with negative esophagoduodenoscopy and colonoscopy.
Initial vital signs were significant for tachycardia 120 bpm, respiratory rate of 31  rpm, oxygen saturation 93% on venti-mask (9 L with FiO2 40%), and blood pressure 140/70  mmHg. On physical examination, the patient was lethargic, only responsive to painful stimuli, decreased breath sounds on auscultation bilaterally with crackles on both lung bases. Initial laboratory workup was significant for white blood cell counts 20,800/mcl, lactic acid of 2.3, HIV nonreactive, and MRSA of the nares positive. Chest X-ray showed extensive patchy consolidation and ground-glass opacities throughout both lung fields with interstitial thickening more pronounced on the right lung base (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the head showed increased hydrocephalus compared to previous CT of the head compatible with shunt failure (Figure 2). Further investigation included ventricular-pleural shunt drainage and thoracentesis of the right-sided pleural effusion for fluid analysis. Initial CSF showed aseptic fluid (Table 1, #1 CSF 1) as well as aseptic pleural fluid. The patient was started on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam for empiric coverage, and the initial diagnosis was altered mental status due to hospital-acquired pneumonia.
During the second day of hospital admission, meningitis/encephalitis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panel was positive for Cryptococcus neoformans (Table 2, CSF 1). Induction therapy with amphotericin B and flucytosine were started, and ventricular-peritoneal shunt fluid analysis was repeated in addition to the antigen titers for confirmation. CSF fluid was reported as aseptic (Table 1, #1 CSF 2) with the persistence of Cryptococcus in the PCR (Table 2, CSF 2) by the third day of hospitalization. Pleural fluid cultures were consistent with the presence of cryptococcal infection as well.
Infectious disease team was consulted, and antimicrobials were tailored to amphotericin B and flucytosine to cover for cryptococcal meningitis and recommendations were made to change the ventricular-pleural shunt. Cryptococcal Ag serum titers were elevated (1 : 20), and fungal cultures later confirmed the presence of C. neoformans only on the pleural fluid by day 5. Through her hospitalization, the patient improved significantly and came back to her usual baseline by day 6, and repeated CSF evaluation was consistent with negative results and repeat fungal cultures did not show growth.
Eventually, during the second week of hospitalization, after confirming the absence of Cryptococcus by fungal culture and PCR, VP shunt was replaced for a ventriculoperitoneal shunt with an external ventricular device with resolving ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus. The patient completed a total of 4 weeks of amphotericin B and flucytosine followed by 8 weeks of fluconazole oral 200  mg.
The patient was transition to the nursing home with close follow up with neurosurgery and infectious disease team.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old bedbound female nursing home resident with a ventriculopleural (VP) shunt presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fluctuating altered mental status, inattention, non-verbal responsiveness, and recurrent fevers up to 101.4 °F (38.5 °C).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 days prior to admission, the patient—who was alert and oriented to person and time at baseline—developed progressive lethargy, unresponsiveness to verbal stimuli, and multiple febrile spikes up to 38.5 °C.
subjective.past_medical_history: Obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a cerebellar tumor with leptomeningeal metastases diagnosed 20 years prior, managed with a ventriculopleural (VP) shunt; seizure disorder; hypertension; hospitalization 2 months prior for suspected GI bleeding with negative EGD and colonoscopy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-day fever (38.5 °C), lethargy, and altered mental status.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: heart rate 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 31 breaths/min, blood pressure 140/70 mmHg, and SpO2 93% on 40% FiO2 Venturi mask (9 L/min). Neurological exam showed lethargy with responsiveness only to painful stimuli; pulmonary auscultation revealed bilaterally decreased breath sounds and bibasilar crackles.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 20,800/µL), lactic acid 2.3 mmol/L, positive nasal MRSA screen, nonreactive HIV serology, and positive serum cryptococcal antigen (titer 1:20). Chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral patchy consolidations, ground-glass opacities, and right-predominant interstitial thickening and pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT demonstrated worsening obstructive hydrocephalus/ventriculomegaly consistent with ventriculopleural shunt failure. Ventriculopleural shunt CSF sampling (days 1 and 3) and right thoracentesis revealed acellular ('aseptic') CSF and pleural fluid chemical profiles, but the CSF FilmArray meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was positive for Cryptococcus neoformans on days 2 and 3, and pleural fluid fungal cultures confirmed growth of Cryptococcus neoformans by day 5.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cryptococcus neoformans ventriculopleural shunt infection, cryptococcal meningitis, and cryptococcal pleuropneumonia causing acute shunt malfunction and hydrocephalus in an HIV-negative 66-year-old female (confirmed by positive CSF Cryptococcus neoformans PCR on days 2 and 3, positive pleural fluid C. neoformans culture on day 5, and serum cryptococcal antigen titer 1:20). Initial empiric vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were switched on day 2 to induction amphotericin B and flucytosine for 4 weeks followed by 8 weeks of oral fluconazole (200 mg daily). By hospital day 6 she returned to her baseline mental status with negative repeat CSF PCR and cultures, and during week 2 her infected ventriculopleural shunt was removed and replaced with an external ventricular drain and subsequent ventriculoperitoneal shunt with resolution of hydrocephalus.
